title: Reaction Rates
seo_title: Reaction Rate Worksheets: Collision Theory, Temperature and Catalysts (High School Chemistry)
standard_text: Apply scientific principles and evidence to provide an explanation about the effects of changing the temperature or concentration of the reacting particles on the rate at which a reaction occurs.
meta_desc: Free high school chemistry worksheets on reaction rates (NGSS HS-PS1-5): collision theory, temperature, concentration, surface area, catalysts and rate data. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Temperature, concentration, surface area and catalysts change how fast a reaction goes.
body_html:
How to think about it

More effective collisions per second means a faster reaction.

  • Particles must collide with enough energy (activation energy) and the right orientation.
  • Faster: higher temperature, higher concentration or pressure, more surface area, a catalyst.
  • Average rate = amount of product (or reactant used) ÷ time.
Example

60 mL of gas in 30 s. Rate?

60 ÷ 30

Answer: 2 mL/s

Example

Why does warm acid react faster?

Faster particles

More energetic collisions

Answer: more effective collisions

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a catalyst is used up.
  • Thinking a faster reaction makes more product.
  • Reading a longer time as a faster reaction.

faq.a: Temperature, concentration (or pressure for gases), surface area and catalysts.

faq.q: How does collision theory explain rates?
faq.a: Reactions happen when particles collide with enough energy and the right orientation. Anything that makes these collisions more frequent speeds up the reaction.

faq.q: How do you calculate an average rate?
faq.a: Divide the amount of product made (or reactant used) by the time taken, for example mL of gas per second.

items.e: Higher oxygen concentration means more collisions.

items.q: How does increasing concentration affect the rate?
c: It increases the rate because collisions are more frequent.

items.q: Why does powdered sugar dissolve and react faster than a sugar cube?
c: Cubes have more particles on the surface.
